title: Buried germanium quantum well proximitised by magnetic field-resilient superconducting platinum iridium germanosilicide
authors: Praveen Viswanathan, Erik Lemmens Sjöstrand, Davide Costa, Marinus Fischer, Athique Ahmed, Sara Martí-Sánchez, Lucas E. A. Stehouwer, Jordi Arbiol, Anasua Chatterjee, Giordano Scappucci, Karina L. Hudson
abstract: Hybrid superconductor-semiconductor systems provide a versatile platform for quantum technologies, ranging from superconducting-spin interfaces to topological quantum devices. Progress toward scalable implementations requires superconductors that exhibit high critical fields ($>1$T) at accessible temperatures integrated with low-disorder semiconductor heterostructures. Here we demonstrate a superconducting platinum iridium germanosilicide (PtIrSiGe), with critical out-of-plane magnetic field up to $B_{\perp} = 1.9$T and critical temperature of $T_c\sim 1.85$K, integrated with planar germanium with mobility $μ= 1.3\times 10^6$cm$^{2}$/Vs via top-down lithography fabrication. We show that the integrity of the germanium quantum well and mobility and density of the 2D hole gas are preserved despite annealing at $500°$C, a temperature comparable to that used for strained germanium epitaxy. We further demonstrate proximitisation of a buried germanium quantum well in a gate-defined Josephson junction/SQUID on a Ge/SiGe heterostructure.
summary: The research reports on fabricating and characterizing a hybrid device coupling a buried germanium quantum well to a robust superconductor ($	ext{PtIrSiGe}$). By achieving proximity superconductivity in this structure using top-down lithography, the authors demonstrate a key technological milestone for building superconducting qubits. The work confirms high performance metrics, including large critical fields and preserved semiconductor quality after processing.
main_problem: Developing superconducting materials integrated with low-disorder semiconductor heterostructures for scalable quantum technologies.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated the proximity effect by coupling a high-mobility germanium quantum well to a robust superconductor ($	ext{PtIrSiGe}$), forming functional Josephson junctions and SQUIDs.
method: Top-down lithography was used to fabricate devices, followed by low-temperature transport measurements (Hall bar, SQUID) and structural characterization using STEM/EDX.
model_or_system: The physical system is a $	ext{Ge}/	ext{SiGe}$ heterostructure containing a buried Germanium Quantum Well ($	ext{Ge QW}$). This semiconductor is proximitized by a superconducting layer of platinum iridium germanosilicide ($	ext{PtIrSiGe}$) to create S-N-S Josephson junctions.
key_observables: Superconducting critical magnetic field ($B_{\perp,c}$), critical temperature ($T_c$), quantum well mobility ($\mu$), and Fraunhofer-like oscillations in the SQUID junction current ($I_{dc}$).
important_parameters: $	ext{PtIrSiGe}$: $B_{\perp,c} \approx 1.9$ T, $T_c \sim 1.85$ K; $	ext{Ge QW}$: $\mu = 1.3 	imes 10^6 	ext{ cm}^2/	ext{Vs}$ at $500^\circ	ext{C}$ annealing.
main_assumptions: The process successfully preserves the structural integrity and high mobility of the Ge QW despite high-temperature processing required for superconductor deposition.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows resistance vs. magnetic field confirming superconductivity limits; Figure 2 details the fabrication cross-section showing alloy diffusion into the heterostructure; Figure 3 displays gate-tunable switching current and SQUID oscillations modulated by $B_{\perp}$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for robust superconducting/semiconductor interfaces, detailing the $	ext{PtIrSiGe}$ material properties, demonstrating its integration via lithography (structural confirmation), and finally proving functionality through electrical measurements on SQUID devices.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the physical realization of solid-state qubits by creating a controllable superconducting interface with high-quality semiconductor channels, which is central to quantum computing hardware development.
